summary: Year 6 learners discover that an equation with two unknowns (e.g. a + b = 12, or 2x + y = 20) has MANY solution pairs, not one. They generate these pairs systematically by fixing one unknown and stepping it through its permitted values in order, computing the partner each time, so no pair is missed or repeated. Stated constraints (such as whole numbers, positive, or within a range) decide which pairs are valid; when values must be whole numbers within limits, the number of pairs is finite and can be counted. This is a precursor to simultaneous equations, where a second equation can usually pin the pair down to one answer.
misconceptions: Treats it like a single-answer equation — finds ONE pair and stops, as if a and b are unique fixed unknowns
Searches unsystematically, so pairs are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
Ignores the constraints — includes 0, negatives, or non-whole values when only positive whole numbers are allowed
For 2x + y = 20 mishandles the coefficient, treating it as x + y (offering pairs like (3, 17))
Cannot say whether the list of pairs is complete

activities.title: Build the pair-finder: sweep one unknown and watch the pairs appear
steps: Before starting, compare a + b = 12 with a + 7 = 12: how many answers does each have? Notice that the one-variable equation has a single answer but the two-unknown equation has many.
Start with a + b = 12 (whole numbers, greater than 0). Set a = 1 and work out b; record (1, 11). Set a = 2 and work out b; record (2, 10). Continue in order: a = 3 → b = 9, a = 4 → b = 8, and so on.
Record each pair in an ordered two-column table (a | b) so completeness is visible.
After listing, answer: 'How many pairs are there? How do you know you have found them ALL?' State the justification: 'I tried every value of a from 1 to 11 in order.'

Optional interactive version: drag a slider for a that moves in whole-number steps from 1 to 11 and watch b recompute live so a + b = 12 always holds; each pair drops into the ordered table AND lights a point on a grid. Sweeping the slider fills the table in order while the separate points line up along a straight line — showing at once that there are many solutions and that stepping a through every permitted value catches them all.
activities.insight: An equation with two unknowns has a whole family of solution pairs; stepping one unknown through its permitted values in order generates every pair and lets you prove the list is complete.

activities.title: Let the constraints bound the count
steps: Reread the stated condition (whole numbers, positive, within a range) and decide which values of a are allowed before listing.
For a + b = 12 with 'whole, greater than 0', check: is (0, 12) allowed? Is (13, −1) allowed? Are decimals allowed? Explain why each is excluded by the condition.
Try a different constraint, e.g. 'a and b are whole numbers from 0 to 10 inclusive', and work out how the list of valid pairs changes and how many remain (a can now only be 2 to 10, so 9 pairs).

Optional interactive version: a constraints toggle ('whole numbers only', 'positive only', 'between 0 and 10') greys out the pairs that break the rule, so the learner SEES how the constraint bounds how many pairs exist.
activities.insight: The constraints bound which values of the stepped unknown are allowed, and therefore exactly how many valid pairs exist.

activities.title: Respect the coefficient: 2x + y = 20
steps: For 2x + y = 20, choose a value for x, then compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly — the 2 doubles x BEFORE y is added.
Find three valid pairs, e.g. x = 1 → y = 18 giving (1,18); x = 2 → y = 16 giving (2,16); x = 3 → y = 14 giving (3,14).
Check a tempting wrong pair: does (3, 17) satisfy 2x + y = 20? Substitute: 2×3 + 17 = 23, not 20. Note that (3, 17) fits x + y = 20, a different equation.
Explain in your own words how 2x + y = 20 differs from x + y = 20.
Optional interactive version: a 2x + y = 20 preset shows y recomputing as 20 − 2x as x changes, making the coefficient's effect visible.
activities.insight: A coefficient changes the partner computation: for 2x + y = 20 the partner is y = 20 − 2x, which is not the same as x + y = 20.

checkQuestion: Here is an equation: a + b = 12, where a and b are whole numbers greater than 0. Find ALL the pairs of numbers that work, and show me how you know you have every one. Then find three different pairs that satisfy 2x + y = 20.
checkAnswer: a + b = 12 (whole, > 0): (1,11), (2,10), (3,9), (4,8), (5,7), (6,6), (7,5), (8,4), (9,3), (10,2), (11,1) — 11 pairs, found by stepping a from 1 to 11; complete because every value of a has been tried in order. For 2x + y = 20: any three pairs with y = 20 − 2x, e.g. (1,18), (2,16), (3,14).
